content: Mechanical ventilation is a common intervention in neonatal intensive care units, but it can cause significant pain and discomfort for newborns. Neonates are particularly sensitive to pain, and this heightened sensitivity may influence both their clinical outcomes and long-term neurodevelopment. Administering medications to alleviate pain could play a critical role in improving survival rates and neurodevelopmental outcomes in these infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of opioid analgesics, such as morphine, compared to placebo, no treatment, or other non-opioid analgesics or sedatives, on various outcomes in mechanically ventilated newborns. These outcomes included pain relief, duration of mechanical ventilation, mortality, growth, and neurodevelopmental progress. The review involved a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies up to June 2007. Additionally, prior reviews and relevant articles were cross-referenced to ensure thoroughness. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared opioids to either a control group or other analgesics or sedatives in neonates undergoing mechanical ventilation. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Categorical outcomes were analyzed using relative risk and risk difference, while continuous outcomes were assessed using weighted mean difference or standardized mean difference. A fixed-effect model was applied for meta-analyses unless significant heterogeneity was detected, in which case a random-effects model was used. The review included 13 studies involving a total of 1,505 infants. The findings indicated that neonates who received opioids had lower Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) scores compared to the control group, with a weighted mean difference of -1.71 (95% confidence interval: -3.18 to -0.24). However, the variability in study design and reporting necessitates cautious interpretation of these results. High levels of heterogeneity were observed in all pain-related analyses, even when lower-quality studies were excluded or the analysis was restricted to very preterm infants. Meta-analyses of other outcomes, including mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, and both shortand long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, did not reveal statistically significant differences between groups. However, very preterm infants who received morphine took significantly longer to achieve full enteral feeding compared to those in the control group, with a weighted mean difference of 2.10 days (95% confidence interval: 0.35 to 3.85). In one study comparing morphine to a sedative, the two treatments resulted in similar pain scores, but morphine was associated with fewer adverse effects. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of opioids in mechanically ventilated newborns. Instead, opioids should be used selectively, guided by clinical judgment and careful assessment of pain indicators. If sedation is deemed necessary, morphine appears to be a safer option than midazolam. Further research is required to better understand the role of opioids in this population. It is also noted that this review has been updated and replaced by a more recent Cochrane review published in 2021.
